title: Bank Reconciliation, Errors and Partnership
lines: This topic mixes several ICom chapters. USAT questions are short: find a bank statement or cash book balance, name an error or pick the correcting entry, work out depreciation or a book value, share partnership profit, or find the due date or proceeds of a bill of exchange.
## Bank reconciliation
The cash book (bank column) and the bank statement rarely agree on the same date. Reasons fall into two groups.
- Timing differences: cheques issued but not yet presented; cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank.
- Items known only to the bank: bank charges, interest, direct credits from customers, dividends collected, dishonoured cheques. These are first entered in the cash book to update it.

Starting from an updated cash book debit balance: add unpresented cheques and deduct uncleared deposits to reach the bank statement balance. Working from the bank statement back to the cash book, do the reverse.
> Cash book debit balance Rs 48,000; unpresented cheques Rs 12,000; uncleared deposits Rs 7,500; bank charges Rs 600 not yet in the cash book.
> Updated cash book = 48,000 − 600 = 47,400

! A favourable balance is a debit in the cash book but a credit on the bank statement. With an overdraft, reverse every adjustment: unpresented cheques make the bank's overdraft smaller, uncleared deposits make it larger.
## Errors and their correction
| Error | Meaning | Trial balance
| Omission | Transaction not recorded at all | Agrees
| Commission | Posted to the wrong account of the same class | Agrees
| Principle | Capital and revenue confused | Agrees
| Original entry | Wrong amount in the book of prime entry | Agrees
| Compensating | Two errors cancel out | Agrees
| One-sided | Wrong side, wrong amount on one side, or casting error | Disagrees

When the trial balance disagrees, the difference is placed in a suspense account on the shorter side. Each error that affected only one side is then corrected with the suspense account as the other half of the entry.
> The sales book is undercast by Rs 1,000. Sales received too little credit.
> Correction: Suspense Dr 1,000; Sales Cr 1,000
! An amount posted to the wrong side must be corrected with twice the amount: once to cancel the wrong entry and once to make the right one.
## Depreciation methods
- Straight-line (fixed instalment): (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Life, equal each year; book value can reach zero or the residual value.
- Reducing balance (diminishing balance): a fixed percentage of the opening book value; the charge falls each year and the book value never reaches zero.
- Land is normally not depreciated. With a provision account, the entry is Depreciation Dr, Provision for Depreciation Cr, and the asset stays at cost.
- On sale: profit or loss = Sale proceeds − Book value (cost − accumulated depreciation).
> Machine Rs 100,000 at 10 % reducing balance: 90,000, then 81,000, then Rs 72,900 after three years.
## Partnership basics

A partnership is an association of persons who share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them. In Pakistan it is governed by the Partnership Act, 1932. Partners have unlimited liability. Their agreement, preferably written as a partnership deed, settles capital, profit-sharing ratio, interest, salaries and drawings.
If there is no agreement, the Act applies:
- Profits and losses are shared equally.
- No interest on capital and no interest on drawings.
- No salary to any partner.
- Interest at 6 % a year on a partner's loan to the firm.

Profit is divided in the profit and loss appropriation account: add interest on drawings, deduct interest on capital and salaries, then share the remainder in the agreed ratio. With fixed capitals these items pass through the partners' current accounts.
> Profit Rs 200,000. Interest on capital 10 %: Faisal 40,000, Ghazala 30,000. Salary to Ghazala 24,000. Remainder 106,000 shared equally, 53,000 each.
> Faisal 93,000; Ghazala 107,000; total 200,000.
## Bills of exchange

A bill of exchange is an unconditional written order, drawn by a creditor (drawer) on a debtor (drawee), to pay a sum on demand or at a fixed future time. The drawee signs to accept it. A promissory note is the reverse: a written promise by the debtor (maker) to pay.
- Due date of a time bill = date plus the period plus 3 days of grace (Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881).
- Drawer, on acceptance: Bills Receivable Dr, Debtor Cr. Drawee: Creditor Dr, Bills Payable Cr.
- Discounting: the bank deducts interest for the unexpired period. Discount = Amount × Rate × Months/12.
- Dishonour: the bill is cancelled and the debtor is again charged with the amount plus any noting charges.
> A bill of Rs 100,000 with three months to run is discounted at 12 % a year.
! For a bill 'after date' counted in days, do not count the date of drawing. A bill of 15 January for 60 days falls on 16 March; with grace, 19 March (in a non-leap year).
## Quick check
- From a cash book debit balance, do you add or deduct unpresented cheques?
- Which errors leave the trial balance in agreement?
- What rate of interest does a partner's loan earn without an agreement?
- How many days of grace are added to a time bill?
